Assemblies that doe the same to divers parts of Christen-

universally by the Pope, and in particular Common-
wealths by Assemblies of the Pastors of the place, (when
the Scripture gives it to none but to Civill Soveraigns,)
comes to be so passionately disputed, that it putteth out
the Light of Nature, and causeth so great a Darknesse
in mens understanding, that they see not who it is to
whom they have engaged their obedience.
Consequent to this claim of the Pope to Vicar Generall And that
of Christ in the present Church, (supposed to be that _ oe
Kingdom of his, to which we are addressed in the Gospel,) 47-75,
is the Doctrine, that it is necessary for a Christian King, genevail :
to receive his Crown by a Bishop; as if it were from
that Ceremony, that he derives the clause of Det gratia
in his title; and that then onely he is made King by
the favour of God, when he is crowned by the authority
of Gods universall Vicegerent on earth; and that every
| Bishop whosoever be his Soveraign, taketh at his Conse-
_ cration an oath of absolute Obedience to the Pope.
Consequent to the same, is the Doctrine of the fourth
Councell of Lateran, held under Pope Innocent the third,
(Chap. 3. de Hereticis.) That if a King at the Popes
admonition, doe not purge his Kingdome of Heresies, and
being excommunicate for the same, doe not give satisfaction
within a year, his Subjects ave absolved of the bond of their
obedience. Where, by Heresies are understood all
opinions which the Church of Rome hath forbidden to
be maintained. And by this means, as often as there [336]
is any repugnancy between the Politicall designes of the
Pope, and other Christian Princes, as there is very often,
there ariseth such a Mist amongst their Subjects, that
they know not a stranger that thrusteth himself into the
throne of their lawfull Prince, from him whom they had
themselves placed there ; and in this Darknesse of mind,
are made to fight one against another, without discerning
their enemies from their friends, under the conduct of
another mans ambition.
